SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology01 / 10
Slide 01

Culture

A system of meanings commonly shared by a group of people

The symbolic aspect of human life

Material Culture

The “stuff” carrying meanings: Jewelry, art, buildings, weapons, machines, hairstyles, clothing, etc.

Nonmaterial Culture

A group’s ways of thinking (beliefs, values, etc) and doing (norms, language, and other forms of interaction).

The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: Languages shape the ways we view the world

Values: Collective ideas/conceptions of what is good, desirable, and proper—or bad, undesirable, and improper

Norms: expected behavior or practices based on values.

Quick Review

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology02 / 10
Functionalist Perspective on Culture

Culture provides a meaning system that fulfills necessary functions in the society and organizations (e.g., corporate culture).

Culture produces unity, identity, order, and predictability. Social crisis is likely to happen if the order of culture is breached too often or too violently.

Dysfunctional cultural practices could become barriers for social change and may cause failures (assets can turn to dysfunctional liabilities).

E.g. “culture of exclusion”, “patriarchal culture”

Like living organisms, cultures find it hard to evolve to another state. Cultures act as a spore—the reproductive cells of plants and micro-organisms—which can stay alive for decades or more after the plant itself has died, in the hope that changes to the environment will bring about another opportunity to flourish.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology03 / 10
The Conflict Perspective on Culture

Classical Conflict Perspective

Social life is an ongoing power struggle, with the privileged try to maintain their advantages while subordinates struggle to fight back.

Dominant groups dominate by encouraging certain cultural understandings that are favorable to them (Antonio Gramsci, Italian Marxist philosopher and communist politician );

The culture that gives legitimacy to the dominance of the dominating groups is known as “hegemony”, or “false consciousness” (for the dominated groups)

Essentially a “class conflict” with a cultural face; culture is the symbolic battleground between the oppressed and the oppressor

The oppressed should overthrow the “oppressive culture”

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology04 / 10
The Conflict Perspective on Culture

E.g., The Chinese Cultural Revolution (1966-1976)

Smash the Four Old Things Movement (1966)

The Four Olds were: Old Ideas, Old Culture, Old Habits, and Old Customs (旧思想, 旧文化, 旧风俗, 旧习惯). These Four Old Things were described as being oppressive, "fostered by the exploiting classes, have poisoned the minds of the people for thousands of years"

Main Targets:

Statues, monuments, historical sites, tombs, historical texts, books, arts for all Emperors, Generals, Political Leaders, Government Officials, Intellectuals, Prominent Social Leaders … before the Communist Regime (1949).

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology07 / 10
Symbolic Interactionism Perspective

Culture as a meaning system is socially constructed – arising from people’s everyday interaction

The meaning system is fluid, with its orders and boundaries constantly being pushed and pulled and redefined.

Cultural conflict stems from the antagonistic interpretation of misalignment between people’s perceptions, not necessarily involve the “oppressed” and the “oppressor”

Culture conflicts, as cultural reconciliations, can be “created”

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology08 / 10
Symbolic Interactionism Perspective

E.g., Thanksgiving Holiday

“I do therefore invite my fellow citizens in every part of the United States, and also those who are at sea and those who are sojourning in foreign lands, to set apart and observe the last Thursday of November next, as a day of Thanksgiving and Praise to our beneficent Father who dwelleth in the Heavens. And I recommend to them that while offering up the ascriptions justly due to Him for such singular deliverances and blessings, they do also, with humble penitence for our national perverseness and disobedience, commend to His tender care all those who have become widows, orphans, mourners or sufferers in the lamentable civil strife in which we are unavoidably engaged, and fervently implore the interposition of the Almighty Hand to heal the wounds of the nation and to restore it as soon as may be consistent with the Divine purposes to the full enjoyment of peace, harmony, tranquility and Union.”

---- Proclamation of Thanksgiving, Abraham Lincoln, 1863

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology09 / 10
Symbolic Interactionism Perspective

Approaches to cultural differences:

Ethnocentrism: A tendency to use our own ways of doing things as a yardstick for judging others (as being odd, undesirable, or unjust);

“One’s own group is the center of everything, and all others are scaled and rated with reference to it”. ----William Sumner

Cultural Relativism: understanding a culture on its own terms; looking at how the elements of a culture fit together.
